summary: Lists requirements for setting up and maintaining point-to-multipoint traffic-engineered MPLS label switched paths. It deliberately avoids solution details. The requirements also cover networks beyond packet switching, such as time-division, wavelength and port switching under GMPLS. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC sets requirements for a planned network path that starts at one router and branches to many destination routers. It explains what signaling solutions must support but does not define one.

questions: what is a p2mp te lsp
what is grafting and pruning in mpls
subtitle: Requirements for signaling traffic-engineered MPLS paths from one source to many receivers

tldr.problem: Existing MPLS traffic-engineering mechanisms described here support point-to-point paths. Building a point-to-multipoint service from separate paths can duplicate traffic or require replication at the source.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists signaling requirements for building and maintaining one-way trees with one ingress and multiple egress routers, including branching, changes, recovery, scalability and security.
tldr.outcome: It specifies requirements rather than a protocol, and says solutions should also be applicable to GMPLS where possible.

today: RFC 4461 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC itself defines requirements and no signaling protocol.

sections.title: Scope and Key Terms
sections.content:
A point-to-multipoint traffic-engineered label switched path (P2MP TE LSP) is a one-way path with one ingress label switching router (LSR) and one or more egress LSRs. A branch LSR sends copies of traffic toward multiple downstream LSRs; a bud LSR is both an egress and a node with downstream LSRs.

The RFC addresses signaling to establish and maintain these paths. It does not specify how a tree is computed, how egress nodes are discovered, or how the traffic-engineering database is built. The requirements are intended to apply to packet-switched MPLS and, where possible, GMPLS networks.
sections.plainLanguage: One router sends traffic along a planned path that can split toward many destination routers. This RFC describes signaling requirements, not how to calculate the route or a protocol that builds it.

sections.title: Why a Branching Path Is Needed
sections.content:
MPLS traffic engineering can reserve resources, apply constraints and support recovery, but the existing mechanisms described in the RFC handle point-to-point LSPs. Multiple point-to-point paths can carry point-to-multipoint traffic, but may cause replication at the ingress or duplicate traffic inside the network.

A P2MP tree lets a branch LSR copy incoming data toward its downstream branches. When receivers are added or removed, a solution should support grafting and pruning parts of the tree without disrupting traffic already flowing on it.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending a separate copy to every destination can waste network capacity. A branching path lets a router copy the traffic where the route splits, and it should allow destinations to join or leave without interrupting others.

sections.title: Tree Shape, Setup and Traffic Rules
sections.content:
A solution must support explicitly routed trees with different shapes, including intermediate routers that both receive traffic and branch it onward. It may allow partially specified routes, but the destination LSRs must be identified. An ingress router must be able to use different tree-computation techniques and explicitly control branch points.

Establishment, maintenance and teardown must scale at least linearly with the number of destinations. Grafting and pruning must not disrupt traffic on the tree. The design must handle signaling information too large for one message without relying on IP fragmentation. The ingress-set attributes, such as bandwidth and priority, must remain consistent across one tree, and solutions must support both shared and exclusive resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need to choose the tree shape and identify its destinations. The signaling must scale with the tree, allow safe changes and keep the service settings consistent from source to every destination.

sections.title: Recovery, Duplication and Scale
sections.content:
Failures that detach destinations or subtrees must be reported upstream. Packet-switched solutions must provide fast protection similar to that available for point-to-point LSPs. Make-before-break re-optimization must be supported so a new route can be established before the old one is removed, including for a subtree alone.

Duplicate traffic can occur briefly during protection or re-optimization, but delivery of duplicates to an application must be limited to bounded temporary conditions. A solution must support both IPv4 and IPv6, coexist with point-to-point paths, and scale no worse than linearly with egress LSRs. The RFC gives an expected initial scale of around a hundred egress LSRs and a working churn figure below 10% per day.
sections.plainLanguage: A failure in one branch should not automatically remove the rest of the tree. During repair, some duplicates may occur briefly, but a solution must prevent them from continuing or reaching applications for long.

sections.title: Security Requirements for Solutions
sections.content:
This requirements document does not define protocol extensions and therefore does not change an existing security model. A solution must support secure establishment and management of P2MP LSPs.

The RFC identifies necessary protections: identify the ingress LSR, allow signaling peers to verify each other's identities, protect control messages against spoofing and tampering, prevent unauthorized branches or leaves, and protect signaling from snooping. Any solution document must include a detailed security section.
sections.plainLanguage: A future signaling protocol must verify who is setting up the path and protect its instructions. It must also stop unauthorized routers from joining the tree.
